l1.name: Reconnaissance
l1.description: Initial reconnaissance is the method of determining targets, (people, assets, services)

l1.name: Weaponization
l1.description: Not Applicable, this action is performed at the attacker side and is invisible to the target organization

l1.name: Delivery
l1.description: Delivery of malicious software to the target organization.

l1.name: Exploitation
l1.description: Initial Exploitation is the first foothold by attackers to an organization, (first stage or second stage exploit).

l1.name: Installation
l1.description: The steps an attacker takes after compromising a target, including elevation of privileges, and installation of backdoors. It enables attackers to remain persistent and use the host as a stepping stone for further actions.

l1.name: Command & Control
l1.description: A communications channel is being set up with the attack to allow remote control over de compromised system

l1.name: Actions on Objectives
l1.description: Any actions taken by the attackers after initial compromise

l1.name: Fraud / Extortion
l1.description: Any tampering of critical business systems which causes or further enables theft of virtual or physical assets via existing or current channels.

l1.name: (D)DoS
l1.description: Any Denial of Service attack, optionally distributed with the goal of causing outages.

l1.name: Physical Access Compromise
l1.description: Any compromise to physical systems information carriers (including documents) and buildings.

l1.name: Blacklisting
l1.description: Any occurrence of external IP addresses on blacklisting sites. Can include blacklists for bots, proxies, mail abuse, etc.

l1.name: Sabotage / Destruction
l1.description: Any action to destroy/damage organizational and personal asset, information or reputation with the goal of causing financial damage or service outages e.g.: social media data posting, doxing, etc.

l1.name: Policy Violations
l1.description: Illegal sites, service account usage, presence of vulnerabilities, Unauthorized process launched, etc..

l2.name: Port Scanning
l2.description: Any scanning of ports to determine potential entry points into the organization

l2.name: Mail probing
l2.description: Any probing attempt via mail to determine valid user accounts

l2.name: Fingerprinting
l2.description: Any attempt to fingerprint devices, systems and applications

l2.name: Passive reconnaissance
l2.description: Reconnaissance activities that are carried out without actively scanning the organization. Mostly through harvesting publically available information

l2.name: Brute force
l2.description: Any attempt to brute force accounts on perimeter

l2.name: Social Engineering
l2.description: Any suspicious emails or calls attempted at eliciting employees to share organizational information

l2.name: Social media harvesting
l2.description: Any attempt to harvest and validate information regarding the organization using social media accounts

l2.name: Web based malware delivery
l2.description: Delivery of malware via malicious web pages, including exploit kits

l2.name: Email based malware delivery
l2.description: Delivery of malware via email

l2.name: Physical malware delivery
l2.description: Delivery of malware via physical means, such as a USB drive

l2.name: Widespread malware outbreak
l2.description: This is a use case that may cover other L2 malware related use cases. Reserved for use in case of multiple outbreaks within a short period, possibly across organizational domains or geographic locations

l2.name: Worm propagation
l2.description: Delivery of malware through automated propagation mechanisms. Such mechanisms are usually vulnerable protocols allowed within the organization

l2.name: Delivery of phishing mail
l2.description: (Attempted) delivery of phishing mails to recipients within the organization, including CEO fraud emails

l2.name: Delivery of Remote Access Tool
l2.description: (Attempted) delivery of a remote access tool to a user within the organization

l2.name: Application whitelist evasion attempt
l2.description: Any attempts to circumvent application whitelisting controls on end-points

l2.name: Network-based attack
l2.description: Network-based attacks aimed at manipulating the information transmitted by the user across the network. This includes session hijacking and MITM attacks

l2.name: Brute force exploitation attempt
l2.description: Attempts to break into accounts and systems by performing a password guessing attack

l2.name: Network intrusion attempt
l2.description: Any direct intrusion attempt into the network, for example by using exploits against systems in the network. Intrusion attempts can be directed at mail servers, web servers or any other internet-facing servers

l2.name: Application intrusion attempt
l2.description: Attempt to exploit a service, possibly resulting in application or service crashes

l2.name: Installation of Remote Access Tool or similar backdoor
l2.description: Any attempt (both successful and failed) to install a Remote Access Tool (RAT) onto an end-point

l2.name: Installation of malware
l2.description: Attempted installation of malware onto an end-point

l2.name: Suspicious outbound network communication
l2.description: Any suspicious network communication to an external destination. This includes C&C traffic, blacklisted resources, unauthenticated proxy requests, wrong DNS servers, malicious payload, new domains, suspicious TLDs, etc.

l2.name: Covert channel
l2.description: Special type of suspicious network communication aimed at circumventing existent security measures. Can include privacy services such as TOR or true covert channels, for example in DNS traffic

l2.name: Data collection
l2.description: Collection of information from within the network in preparation of data exfiltration. Collection always involves transfer of information to a central location

l2.name: Data exfiltration
l2.description: Exfiltration of information to outside the perimeter by attackers. This could be customer information or sensitive corporate information. Exfiltration can be done via the network or via USB drives

l2.name: Credential theft
l2.description: Stealing account credential from password databases, plain-text files or network sources. May include passive network sniffing of credentials due to usage of insecure communication protocols

l2.name: Internal reconnaissance
l2.description: Internal reconnaissance is carried out by attackers after initial compromise to find systems and information that can be used to perform lateral movement

l2.name: Lateral movement
l2.description: Lateral movement is the movement of attackers from the initial compromise to another system. Attackers will try to move to always-on systems that have more network access than the system that was initially compromised

l2.name: Internal Brute force
l2.description: This use case is reserved for brute force attacks after initial compromise. This kind of activity supports the attackers in lateral movement

l2.name: Privilege escalation
l2.description: Any attempts to obtain higher privileges on the system by the attacker, for example through modification of the account or group

l2.name: File corruption, encryption and unauthorized access
l2.description: This activity could be due to a ransomware attack or due to a an attacker in the network either looking for sensitive information or seeking to destroy documents

l2.name: Account breached
l2.description: Any indications that an account on a system or application was compromised. This includes pass-the-hash attacks

l2.name: Installation of persistence mechanism
l2.description: Persistence mechanisms are used to by the attackers so that they can return to the compromised system at any time. Persistence mechanisms include registry keys and applications run at startup

l2.name: Database compromise attempt
l2.description: Any attempts to compromise a database or database account

l2.name: Detection evasion techniques
l2.description: Any attempts to remove indications of malicious activity by the attacker himself. This can include sabotage of the target system or removal of audit logs. This also includes other detection evasion techniques

l2.name: Cloud Service or Account compromise
l2.description: Any indications that a cloud service (SaaS) or account was compromised and is actively being used to either obtain sensitive information or to move laterally into the company internal perimeter

l2.name: Usage of remote access tool
l2.description: Usage of remote access tool on host. These tools are used to remotely access and use the compromised system

l2.name: Rogue network device or service
l2.description: A new network device or network service could be introduced into the network for purposes of information gathering and lateral movement. New devices could be virtual machines, while new services include DNS, Proxy and DHCP services

l2.name: Multiple AO categories
l2.description: This category is reserved for situations in which a single host . Usually, this category is used by generic anomaly detection tools or security monitoring overlays (e.g. multiple alerts from a single device)

l2.name: Extortion attempts
l2.description: Any attempts by attackers to gain financial compensation from the organization by not taking action. Such action may include DDoS attacks or sensitive information disclosure

l2.name: CEO Fraud
l2.description: Attempts by criminals to impersonate the organization's CEO or other board-level executive and to have the victim transfer large amounts of money. Usually carried out by sending spoofed email or by business email compromise

l2.name: Volume DDoS
l2.description: DDoS attack conducted by directing high volumes of (spoofed) traffic to out organization’s network

l2.name: Protocol (D)Dos
l2.description: DDoS attack using protocol anomalies. Some network equipment or firewalls cannot effectively deal with some types of protocol attacks. Most commonly, this results in resource exhaustion

l2.name: Application (D)DoS
l2.description: (D)Dos attack conducted by mimicking high volumes of legitimate traffic to our web application servers

l2.name: Illegal entry into datacenter
l2.description: Physical access compromise by an attacker into the data center

l2.name: Illegal entry into office space
l2.description: Physical access compromise by an attacker into the office space

l2.name: Mobile device lost or stolen
l2.description: Mobile device, such as a tablet or a phone lost or stolen

l2.name: Anomalous access token usage
l2.description: Any anomalous usage of access tokens, such as entry badges

l2.name: Physical network access compromise
l2.description: This is usually placement of a physical rogue device in the network. Such a device could be a wireless access point (WAP) or any other device, including Raspberry pi

l2.name: IP blacklisting
l2.description: Note that backlisting may occur from resource abuse, but requires a different response as the entry must be removed from the blacklist as soon as possible to avoid further reputational damage

l2.name: Mail server blacklisting
l2.description: Any occasion where an organizational email server was blacklisted, possibly due to sending spam or malicious email

l2.name: Cyber sabotage
l2.description: Sabotage or destruction of a system through means of computer. This can be done as part of a cover-up strategy or simply to disrupt business.

l2.name: Physical sabotage
l2.description: Physical sabotage of an asset. This is physical damage directly from the attacker, or physical damage as a result of industrial sabotage. In case of ICS, sabotage can lead to physical destruction and thus have safety impact as well.

l2.name: Defacement
l2.description: Defacement of (most likely) organizational websites. Usually conducted by hacktivist actors

l2.name: Illegal content streaming or usage of disallowed web service
l2.description: This could be copyrighted material, but also includes other illegal categories

l2.name: Insecure communication protocol
l2.description: Usage of protocols that are outdated and unsecure. Examples of such protocols are FTP and telnet

l2.name: Vulnerable system or service
l2.description: Any vulnerable systems or applications / services that leave the system vulnerable for compromise

l2.name: Unauthorized process launched
l2.description: Launch of an unauthorized process. Examples of such processes are psexec, powershell and the command prompt. Also covers unauthorized processes running as a service

l2.name: Illegal or aberrant application found on host
l2.description: Any application present on hosts that are not allowed by policy or are quite simply illegal. Examples of such applications are hacking tools and pirated software

l2.name: Resource abuse
l2.description: This use case is reserved for situations where systems are being abused, for example for bitcoin mining

l2.name: Unauthorized use of high-privileged account
l2.description: Any unauthorized use of accounts with high privileges, such as root accounts on Linux / UNIX and administrator accounts on Windows

l2.name: Unauthorized modification of technical policy
l2.description: Unauthorized modification of configuration settings. This can be a compliance issue, where the configuration may result in a hardening baseline deviation. It can also be part of malicious activity

business_drivers.name: Direct Financial Loss
business_drivers.description:
Prevent Loss due to Financial theft
Prevent Loss due to Theft of IP
Prevent Loss due to Fraud
Prevent Loss due to Sabotage

business_drivers.name: Reputational Damage
business_drivers.description:
Prevent Reputational damage due to loss of information (customer information, etc.)
Prevent Reputational damage due to (Perceived) lack of information security

business_drivers.name: Legal and Regulatory Obligations
business_drivers.description:
Avoid missed business opportunities due to regulator limitations 
Prevent penalties due to missed regulator requirements

business_drivers.name: Enable Business
business_drivers.description:
Assist and enable business to use new channels and methods in order to be competative
Reduce risk by implementing Security Monitoring and Response

business_drivers.name: Business Continuity
business_drivers.description:
Early detection of threats to provide business continuity
Prevent business against data loss (deletion)
Prevent outages of critical business services

business_drivers.name: Strategic and Commercial interests
business_drivers.description: Damage to strategic and commercial interests, e.g. misleading management information, inefficient operation, disadavantage in negotiations etc.

threat_actor.name: Professional Criminals
threat_actor.description: Actors that perform malicious activity to make money. These criminals have revenue models, ranging from selling malware to DDoS extortion threat and stealing money using banking malware.

threat_actor.name: State Actors
threat_actor.description: Actors that perform malicious activity on behalf of their country. Such activities are usually espionage, but may also include disruption of critical infrastructure of another country. These actors have a lot of capabilities and the resources and perseverance to carry out long and covert operations.

threat_actor.name: Terrorists
threat_actor.description: Actors that perform malicious activity to support terrorist organizations in their cause. Their activities will usually focus on disruption through DDoS attacks and defacement. Generally speaking, these actors do not have a lot of capabilities.

threat_actor.name: Hacktivists, Cyber vandals and Script Kiddies
threat_actor.description: Hacktivist actors have similar activities as terrorist actors, but a different motive.  Capabilities depend on the hacktivist group and composition. Cyber vandals and script kiddies usually carry out the activities for personal recognition. Their capabilities vary, but resources are limited.

threat_actor.name: Internal Actors
threat_actor.description: Actors that perform their activities from within the organization. This may include unintentional behavior, but can also originate from a grudge against the employer.

threat_actor.name: Private Organizations
threat_actor.description: Actors from other organizations. The CSAN differentiates 3 motives: attacking confidentiality for financial gain, improve their competitive position or to use (personal) data collected without consent.

threat_actor.name: Multiple Actors
threat_actor.description: Multiple primary actors may carry out this malicious activity

detection_technology.name: SIEM
detection_technology.description: Security Information and Event Management system. Such systems are usually key to SOC detection capabilities

detection_technology.name: Big data analytics
detection_technology.description: A big data platform to gather information from the network that can be used for anomaly detection and hunting capabilities

detection_technology.name: NIDS/NIPS
detection_technology.description: Network Intrusion Detection (or Prevention) System. Network-based protection or detection mechanism that identifies attacks on the network.

detection_technology.name: HIPS
detection_technology.description: Host Intrusion Detection (or Prevention) System. Host-based protection or detection mechanism that identifies attacks against the host.

detection_technology.name: Anti-malware
detection_technology.description: Host-based protection mechanism that protects against malware threats.

detection_technology.name: Network anomaly detection
detection_technology.description: Detection technology that uses network information (for example: flows) to detect aberrant behavior

detection_technology.name: Email protection
detection_technology.description: Systems protecting from email-based threats, mostly malicious attachments

log_source.name: Firewall
log_source.description: Logging from firewall devices. Usually, these are network firewalls. Host-based firewalls may also provide logging. Such logging contains connections made by possible attackers and can be used to identify network-based attacks, such as session attacks and scanning

log_source.name: Network traffic
log_source.description: Actual network traffic. This can be netflow data, or actual traffic. Can be analyzed for network based anomalies

log_source.name: OS logging
log_source.description: Logging from Operating Systems. This can include both server and client OS logging. Should include at least system and security events that may carry indicators of attacks against these systems.

log_source.name: Application log
log_source.description: Logging from applications. Such logging is usually very specific and diverse. May be used in big data systems for analytics purposes and anomaly detection.

log_source.name: Web application logging
log_source.description: Logging from web applications. Since many attacks against websites are conducted at the application level, this logging may carry evidence of such attacks.

log_source.name: Database log
log_source.description: Logging from databases. May include both security logging as well as database change logging

log_source.name: Proxy log
log_source.description: Logging from network proxy systems, that are used to connect users to the internet

scope.name: VIPs
scope.description: A selection of important users in the enterprise. Such users may include C-level executives, but also key personnel with access to sensitive systems and crown jewels

scope.name: Administrators
scope.description: Only administrative users with high privileges

scope.name: Business critical assets
scope.description: A selection of systems which are deemed critical to the enterprise

scope.name: Business critical applications
scope.description: A selection of applications which are deemed critical to the enterprise (i.e. a high confidentiality, integrity and availability classification). These applications should reside on business critical assets

scope.name: Business critical databases
scope.description: A selection of databases which are deemed critical to the enterprise. These databases should reside on business critical assets

scope.name: Public network
scope.description: Networks within the enterprise that can be accessed and used publically

scope.name: Restricted networks
scope.description: A selection of networks within the enterprise that are restricted due to the sensitive nature of assets residing in that network

scope.name: Datacenter networks
scope.description: The network within the datacenter. Usually, this network

scope.name: Wireless networks
scope.description: Any wireless networks within the network, with the exception of public networks

scope.name: Office networks
scope.description: All networks that are used for office purposes, including printer networks

scope.name: Office location
scope.description: All physical office locations, with the exception of the main office

scope.name: Datacenter location
scope.description: The physical location of a datacenter

scope.name: Main office location
scope.description: The physical location of the main office
